title: Gaviscon and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Take After Drinking?
excerpt: Can you take Gaviscon after drinking? How the alginate raft works, why alcohol causes heartburn, how it compares with Mylanta, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you take Gaviscon after drinking? How it works with alcohol-related heartburn, Gaviscon vs Mylanta, ingredient cautions, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no known dangerous interaction between Gaviscon and alcohol. For most healthy adults, taking a normal dose of Gaviscon for heartburn after a night of drinking is fine. The catch is that alcohol is usually what's *causing* the heartburn, so Gaviscon is treating the symptom while the drink keeps feeding the problem. The ingredients also matter more than most people realize: some Gaviscon products are high in sodium, the aluminum and magnesium versions need care if you have kidney problems, and every antacid can interfere with other medicines you take.

**The quick rules:** Take the labeled dose, not more. Take it after you've eaten if you can, since that's when it works best. Keep it about two hours apart from your other medicines. Don't use it as a way to keep drinking through heartburn. And if your "heartburn" comes with vomiting blood, black stools, severe stomach pain, or chest pain that feels like pressure, skip the antacid and get medical help.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how Gaviscon and alcohol affect your stomach in general terms. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using Gaviscon if** you have kidney disease, heart failure, high blood pressure, or are on a low-sodium diet; you take prescription medicines every day; you are pregnant or breastfeeding; or you find yourself needing antacids more than twice a week. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe or worsening stomach pain, or have chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw.

## How Gaviscon Works (and Why It's Different From Other Antacids)

Most antacids, like Tums or Rolaids, do one thing: they neutralize stomach acid on contact. Gaviscon's main selling point is that it adds a second action, a physical barrier.

The key ingredient is **alginate**, a substance extracted from brown seaweed. When it meets stomach acid, it turns into a thick gel. Most Gaviscon formulas also contain a carbonate or bicarbonate, which gives off small bubbles of carbon dioxide when it hits acid. Those bubbles get trapped in the gel and make it float. The result is a foamy layer that sits on top of whatever is in your stomach, often called a **"raft."**

That raft does two useful things:

1. **It acts as a lid.** Heartburn happens when stomach contents push back up through the valve at the top of the stomach into the esophagus (the tube to your throat). The raft sits right at that spot, so what rises tends to be the gel rather than acid.
2. **It neutralizes some acid.** The antacid ingredients in the mix reduce acidity directly, especially in the pocket of acid that tends to collect at the top of the stomach after a meal.

Because the raft floats on stomach contents, Gaviscon tends to work best **after eating**, when there's something for it to float on. That's why many labels say to take it after meals and at bedtime.

### Not every "Gaviscon" is the same product

This trips a lot of people up. The name is used for different formulas in different countries:

- **In the UK and much of Europe**, Gaviscon products are built around sodium alginate. Gaviscon Original contains sodium alginate, sodium bicarbonate, and calcium carbonate. Gaviscon Advance uses sodium alginate with potassium bicarbonate. Gaviscon Double Action pairs alginate with extra calcium carbonate for more acid neutralizing.
- **In the US**, the common Gaviscon products are mainly aluminum hydroxide and magnesium antacids (magnesium carbonate or magnesium trisilicate), with alginate included as part of the formula.

The ingredient list changes the cautions that apply to you, so always read the label of the exact product in your hand. If you're traveling, don't assume the box you buy abroad matches the one at home.

## Gaviscon and Alcohol: Is There an Interaction?

There is no well-documented chemical interaction between Gaviscon and alcohol. Gaviscon's ingredients mostly stay in your digestive tract. They aren't processed by the liver the way acetaminophen is, and they don't add sedation the way some sleep aids or antihistamines do. That's why the combination isn't considered dangerous for most people.

The more useful question is how alcohol and Gaviscon interact in your *stomach*, and that's where the real story is.

### How alcohol causes heartburn in the first place

Alcohol makes reflux more likely in several ways at once:

- **It relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach.** That ring of muscle (the lower esophageal sphincter) normally stays tight to keep acid down. Alcohol loosens it, so stomach contents can slip back up more easily.
- **It slows the esophagus.** Alcohol can weaken the wave-like squeezing that normally clears acid back down into the stomach, so acid lingers where it burns.
- **It irritates the stomach lining.** Drinking, especially a lot at once or on an empty stomach, can inflame the lining of the stomach (gastritis), which feels like burning, gnawing, or a sour ache.
- **It tends to come with other triggers.** Big late meals, fatty or spicy food, carbonated mixers, and going to bed soon after the last drink all add to reflux.

So Gaviscon can still do its job when alcohol is involved. It'll form its barrier and calm some acid. But while you keep drinking, the alcohol keeps loosening the valve and irritating the lining, so the relief may be shorter and weaker than you'd get from heartburn after a normal meal. For a deeper look at what's going on, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).

### Can alcohol make Gaviscon less effective?

There isn't good research on whether alcohol itself breaks down the raft, so be wary of anyone who claims it definitely does or doesn't. What we can say is practical: a single dose of Gaviscon has a limited capacity, and if you keep drinking afterward you're creating new reflux on top of it. Taking more doses than the label allows won't fix that, and it raises the risk of side effects from the sodium, aluminum, magnesium, or calcium in the product.

## The Real Cautions: It's About the Ingredients

Because there's no direct alcohol interaction, the safety questions are mostly about what's in your particular Gaviscon and how it fits with the rest of your health.

### Sodium

Several Gaviscon formulas, especially the UK sodium alginate and sodium bicarbonate liquids, contain a meaningful amount of sodium per dose. The amount is listed on the leaflet. For most people taking a dose or two, this doesn't matter. It does matter if you've been told to limit salt for high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease. A night of drinking often comes with salty food already, so this can add up. Formulas that use potassium bicarbonate instead lower the sodium, but potassium has its own cautions for people with kidney problems.

### Aluminum and magnesium

The US-style aluminum hydroxide and magnesium formulas are generally safe for occasional use. The issues show up with regular, heavy use or kidney trouble:

- **Magnesium** can cause loose stools. After drinking, when your gut may already be upset, that can make diarrhea worse. (See our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) for why alcohol does this.)
- **Aluminum** tends to cause constipation.
- **If your kidneys don't work well,** both aluminum and magnesium can build up in your body. That's why antacid labels tell people with kidney disease to ask a doctor first.

### Calcium carbonate

Calcium carbonate is in several Gaviscon versions and in Tums. Occasional use is fine. Very large amounts over time can cause problems with calcium levels and kidney function, which is one reason the label sets a daily maximum. Don't stack Gaviscon on top of several rolls of Tums because the first one "didn't work."

### Other medicines

This is the caution people most often miss. Antacids, including Gaviscon, can reduce how well some medicines are absorbed when taken at the same time. Examples commonly listed on antacid labels and leaflets include certain antibiotics (such as tetracyclines and some quinolones), iron supplements, thyroid medicine, and some heart and blood-pressure drugs. The usual advice is to **keep Gaviscon about two hours apart from other medicines**. If you take something every day, ask a pharmacist how to time them.

## Mylanta and Alcohol

Mylanta is a close cousin and often sits on the same shelf, so it's worth covering here.

Mylanta is a traditional antacid. Most Mylanta liquids combine magnesium hydroxide with either aluminum hydroxide or calcium carbonate, and many add **simethicone**, which helps break up gas bubbles to ease bloating. Unlike Gaviscon, it doesn't rely on an alginate raft. It works by neutralizing acid.

Like Gaviscon, Mylanta has **no known direct interaction with alcohol**. The same practical points apply:

- It treats the burn, not the cause, so relief may fade if you keep drinking.
- The magnesium can loosen stools, which matters if your stomach is already unsettled after drinking.
- People with kidney disease should check with a doctor before using it.
- Keep it about two hours apart from other medicines.

**Gaviscon vs Mylanta after drinking:** if your main problem is acid rising into your throat, a sour taste, or heartburn that's worse when you lie down, Gaviscon's raft is designed for exactly that. If you feel more of a general sour, gassy, bloated stomach, Mylanta's antacid-plus-simethicone combination may suit you better. Both are reasonable for occasional use. Neither should become a nightly habit without talking to a doctor, because needing an antacid every time you drink is a sign worth looking into. For a side-by-side look at the main options, see our guide to the [best antacid after drinking](/never-hungover/best-antacid-after-drinking).

## How to Use Gaviscon Safely After Drinking

If you've had a few drinks and the heartburn shows up, here's a sensible approach:

1. **Stop drinking for the night.** This does more than any antacid. Every additional drink keeps loosening that valve.
2. **Eat something plain if you haven't.** Gaviscon's raft works best on top of food, and food also buffers acid. Toast, crackers, rice, or a banana are easy options. Avoid greasy or spicy snacks.
3. **Take the labeled dose.** Shake liquids well. For chewable tablets, chew thoroughly rather than swallowing whole.
4. **Stay upright for a couple of hours.** Lying flat right after drinking and eating makes reflux worse. If you need to sleep, raising the head of your bed or lying on your left side may help.
5. **Sip water.** It helps with dehydration, and small sips can wash acid back down. Skip more fizzy drinks, which add gas and pressure.
6. **Separate it from other medicines.** If you need a painkiller or your regular pills, leave a gap of about two hours where you can.

### What about taking it before you drink?

Some people take Gaviscon before a night out to try to head off heartburn. At the labeled dose, this is unlikely to hurt a healthy adult. But there is no good evidence that taking Gaviscon before drinking prevents alcohol-related reflux, and it has no effect on a hangover. It also doesn't slow how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream in any meaningful way, so don't treat it as a "lining your stomach" trick. A real meal before drinking does a better job on both fronts. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why food matters so much.

## Gaviscon for a Hangover: What It Can and Can't Do

A hangover is a bundle of different problems: dehydration, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach and gut, inflammation, low blood sugar, and the after-effects of breaking down alcohol. Gaviscon only touches one piece of that.

**It can help with:**

- Heartburn and acid reflux the morning after
- A burning or sour feeling in the chest or throat
- Some general stomach discomfort from acid

**It won't help with:**

- Headache
- Tiredness and brain fog
- Dehydration
- Nausea that isn't caused by acid (Gaviscon isn't an anti-nausea medicine)
- Shakiness or a racing heart

If nausea is your main problem, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025). If your whole stomach is upset, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) covers the common causes and what helps.

### A note on painkillers

Many people reach for both an antacid and a painkiller the morning after. Be careful with ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin. They can irritate the stomach lining and raise the risk of stomach bleeding, and alcohol already does the same, so the burning you're treating with Gaviscon could get worse. Antacids can mask that irritation rather than prevent it. If you need a painkiller, take it with food, stick to the label dose, and read our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) first, since each has its own risks after drinking.

## How Gaviscon Compares to Other Heartburn Options

Here's a simple way to think about the main over-the-counter choices after drinking:

| Option | How it works | Speed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gaviscon** | Alginate raft plus antacid | Fast | Reflux and heartburn, especially when lying down |
| **Tums / Mylanta** | Neutralizes acid on contact | Fast, short-lived | Quick relief of occasional heartburn |
| **Pepcid (famotidine)** | Reduces how much acid your stomach makes | Slower to start, lasts longer | Heartburn you expect to last hours |
| **Omeprazole (Prilosec)** | Strongly reduces acid production | Takes a day or more for full effect | Frequent heartburn, as a short course |

A few points worth knowing:

- **Gaviscon and Tums** both work fast, which makes them the usual first choice for heartburn that's already started. See [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) for more on calcium carbonate.
- **Pepcid** takes longer to kick in but lasts longer. Some people take it before an evening they know will trigger heartburn. Our guide to [Pepcid and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepcid-and-alcohol) covers whether that's a good idea.
- **Omeprazole** isn't for quick relief. It's for frequent heartburn and usually takes a few days to work fully. See [omeprazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/omeprazole-and-alcohol).
- **Pepto-Bismol** is a different kind of product, used more for upset stomach and diarrhea. It contains a salicylate related to aspirin, so read [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) before combining it with anything else.

Combining a fast antacid like Gaviscon with a slower acid reducer like Pepcid is something pharmacists sometimes suggest for short-term use, but check with one first if you're taking anything else regularly.

## When Heartburn After Drinking Needs a Doctor

For most social drinkers, heartburn after a big night is uncomfortable but harmless, and it goes away once the alcohol and the rich food clear. Some symptoms are different, though, and an antacid is the wrong response.

> **When to see a doctor.** **Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you have:** vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds; black, tarry, or bloody stools; severe stomach pain, especially pain that spreads to your back or keeps getting worse; chest pain that feels like pressure, squeezing, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain in your arm, jaw, or back; or you feel faint or confused. Heart symptoms can feel like heartburn, so if you aren't sure, get checked. **See a doctor soon if:** you need antacids more than twice a week; heartburn lasts more than two weeks even with treatment; you have trouble or pain when swallowing, or food feels stuck; you're losing weight without trying; or you're over 55 and getting new or worsening heartburn.

A couple of these deserve a short explanation:

- **Severe upper stomach pain that spreads to the back** after heavy drinking can be a sign of pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas that needs medical treatment. It is not something to manage with antacids at home.
- **Vomiting blood after repeated vomiting** can come from a tear in the lining where the esophagus meets the stomach. Small streaks can happen, but any significant amount of blood needs to be checked.
- **Heartburn that keeps coming back** may mean you have acid reflux disease (GERD). Treating it properly matters, because long-term untreated reflux can damage the esophagus. A doctor can help you work out whether alcohol, food, weight, or something else is the main driver.

If you notice that you're getting heartburn every time you drink, that's useful information. Cutting back, switching drinks, or changing when and what you eat with alcohol often helps more than any medicine.

## Practical Ways to Get Less Heartburn When You Drink

Gaviscon works better when you're not fighting your own habits. These are the changes with the most practical value:

- **Eat a real meal first,** but not a huge, greasy one right before bed.
- **Slow down.** Alternate each alcoholic drink with water.
- **Watch your triggers.** Many people find wine, especially white wine, and carbonated drinks like beer, champagne, and soda mixers are the worst for reflux. Notice what bothers you.
- **Stop drinking a few hours before bed** so you're not lying down with a stomach full of alcohol and food.
- **Raise the head of your bed** if night-time reflux is common for you.
- **Have fewer drinks.** It's not exciting, but the amount you drink matters more than any other factor.

For a broader set of evidence-backed habits, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing, food, hydration, and sleep.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

Some people who drink socially also use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for how it affects alcohol's effects in the body. It's worth being clear about what it does and doesn't do here:

- **DHM is not an antacid** and there is no good evidence that it helps with heartburn or reflux. If heartburn is your problem, Gaviscon or another antacid is the right tool.
- Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright.
- There's no known interaction between DHM and Gaviscon, but if you take any supplement alongside antacids, keeping them a couple of hours apart is a simple precaution, the same as with other medicines.

If you're curious about trying it for the rest of the hangover picture, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what to check before combining it with other medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Gaviscon and alcohol don't have a direct dangerous interaction, and taking Gaviscon for heartburn after drinking is reasonable for most healthy adults. It works by forming a floating gel layer that helps keep acid out of your throat, plus some acid neutralizing. What it can't do is stop alcohol from causing the reflux in the first place, so the best results come from stopping drinking, eating something plain, staying upright, and taking the labeled dose. Check the ingredients of your specific product if you watch your salt intake or have kidney problems, keep it two hours apart from other medicines, and treat vomiting blood, black stools, severe stomach pain, or pressure-like chest pain as reasons to get medical help, not reasons to reach for another dose.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take Gaviscon after drinking alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There is no known direct chemical interaction between Gaviscon and alcohol, and the ingredients mostly stay in the gut rather than being absorbed. Take the labeled dose, ideally after you've eaten something, and don't use it to keep drinking through heartburn. If you have kidney disease, are on a low-sodium diet, or take other regular medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

**Does alcohol stop Gaviscon from working?**

Not in any way that's been well studied. Gaviscon will still form its protective layer and neutralize some acid. The problem is that alcohol keeps causing the reflux in the first place, by relaxing the valve at the top of your stomach and irritating the lining. If you keep drinking, the heartburn tends to keep coming back, and a single dose can only do so much.

**Can I take Gaviscon before drinking to prevent heartburn?**

Some people do, and it's unlikely to cause harm at the labeled dose. But there is no good evidence that taking Gaviscon before drinking prevents alcohol-related heartburn, and it does nothing for a hangover. Eating a proper meal, drinking more slowly, avoiding lying down soon after drinking, and having fewer drinks are more reliable ways to cut down reflux.

**Is Gaviscon or Mylanta better after drinking?**

They do slightly different jobs. Mylanta is a classic antacid that neutralizes acid. Gaviscon adds alginate, which forms a gel layer on top of your stomach contents that helps block acid from rising into your throat, so it's often preferred for reflux and heartburn when lying down. Both are fine for occasional use after drinking. Neither is designed for long-term daily use without a doctor's advice.

**How long after drinking can I take Gaviscon?**

There's no required waiting period. Gaviscon can be taken when heartburn starts, including after drinking. The general timing on many labels is after meals and at bedtime, which matches when reflux tends to be worst. The more important timing rule is to keep it about two hours apart from other medicines, because antacids can reduce how well some drugs are absorbed.

**Can Gaviscon help a hangover?**

Only with one part of it. If your hangover includes heartburn, acid reflux, or a sour, burning stomach, Gaviscon can ease that. It won't help headache, tiredness, dehydration, poor sleep, or nausea from other causes. Water, food, rest, and time do most of the work for a hangover.

**When is heartburn after drinking a sign of something serious?**

Get urgent medical help for vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, severe or worsening stomach pain (especially pain that spreads to your back), chest pain that feels like pressure or comes with shortness of breath or sweating, or trouble swallowing. See a doctor soon if you need antacids more than twice a week, or if symptoms last more than two weeks despite treatment.
